question: The recent World Health Organization (WHO) policy brief entitled ‘Effective regulatory frameworks for ending inappropriate marketing of breast-milk substitutes and foods for infants and young children’ finds that EU Member States score only 39 / 100 in alignment with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes.

According to the WHO, this is due to the limited scope of EU legislation, which currently only regulates infant formula for children under 12 months of age, while leaving follow-on formula, toddler milks and most complementary foods outside its remit.

The WHO highlights widespread and inappropriate promotion and cross-promotion practices, the absence of rules addressing marketing in healthcare settings and conflicts of interest, the lack of nutrient profile standards for complementary foods, and the absence of effective monitoring and enforcement mechanisms in the EU.

In the light of these findings and their potential impact on early childhood nutrition, breastfeeding rates and public health: Is Commission considering requesting updated scientific and policy advice from the European Food Safety Authority and WHO, and subsequently proposing legislative measures to expand the scope of EU rules to all breast-milk substitutes and foods for infants and young children up to 36 months of age, prohibiting cross-promotion, addressing conflicts of interest in healthcare settings, establishing nutrient profile standards, and introducing mandatory EUwide monitoring and enforcement mechanisms?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.2.2026) EU food law governs the labelling, presentation, advertising, promotional and commercial practices for infant and follow-on formula, in line with the principles of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes.

Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1271 restricts the advertising of infant formula to publications specialising in baby care and scientific journals requiring that their content be scientific and factual, without suggesting bottle-feeding equals or surpasses breastfeeding. The Regulation also allows Member States to further restrict or prohibit advertising of infant formula.
Member States are primarily responsible for the correct application of EU food law and must ensure that the requirements of EU food law are respected.

In line with the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) advice on sugar intake, the Commission is working on revising compositional requirements for processed cereal-based foods and baby foods taking into account concerns over excessive intake of sugars.

The Commission is following developments after a resolution2 by the World Health Assembly that urges WHO member states to reinforce regulations and monitoring for marketing breastmilk substitutes and foods for young children. The WHO Director-General is to report on this resolution's implementation at the Eighty-first World Health Assembly in 2028 as part of the maternal, infant, and young child nutrition plan.
The Commission is closely following the WHO work and may consider proposing regulatory adjustments, if appropriate.
1 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/127 of 25 September 2015 supplementing Regulation (EU) No

609/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the specific compositional and information requirements for infant formula and follow-on formula and as regards requirements on information relating to infant and young child feeding. OJ L 25, 2.2.2016, p. 1. 2 World Health Organization, Seventy-Eighth World Health Assembly WHA78/18.
